Lessons.Title: Addition and Subtraction
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: flexibly choose appropriate strategies for addition AND subtraction of decimals, not always performing a standard algorithm. The source asks students to explain why a place-value approach is better for some expressions and counting up or compensation for close values; there is also an optional set of larger decimal differences.

Warm-up: compare two ways to find 70.00−68.75: subtract using a correctly aligned vertical algorithm or add up 0.25 to 69 and 1.00 more to 70. Explain why the counting-up method is efficient when the two numbers are close, while for some unrelated numbers a place-value algorithm is clearer.

Activity 1 — subtraction choice: find 8.24−3.7=4.54, 102.5−8.06=94.44 and 52.00−51.68=0.32. For 8.24−3.70, a place-value subtraction may be straightforward; for 52−51.68, counting up via +0.32 may be shorter. Require the learner to state which decimal places are aligned and why their chosen method is sensible.

Activity 2 — mix operations: calculate 41.36−5.2=36.16, 120+24.85=144.85, 120−24.85=95.15, and 308.57+64.8=373.37. Compare strategies, including compensation when subtracting a quantity close to 25 or adding one close to 65. Optional challenge: compute 260.14−259.6=0.54 by counting up, and explain why a complicated subtraction layout is not mandatory.

Assessment: the official tasks emphasize strategy choice, interpretation of digit places, and comparing another student's reasoning. Exact sums/differences are automatable subskills but do not prove a student selected or justified a valid strategy. Original student drawings and protected response are not reproduced.

KeyConcepts.Title: Flexible decimal method selection
KeyConcepts.Definition: Place-value algorithms, counting up and compensation may all calculate an exact decimal result.
KeyConcepts.Example: The best strategy depends on the structure of the numbers.

KeyConcepts.Title: Align decimal places for both operations
KeyConcepts.Definition: Add or subtract units of the same magnitude, writing missing hundredths as zero.
KeyConcepts.Example: Do not align the final digit of unequal-precision decimals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Check differences by addition
KeyConcepts.Definition: A valid subtraction result plus its subtrahend returns the starting quantity.
KeyConcepts.Example: The inverse provides an independent arithmetic check.

WorkedExamples.Title: Close decimals
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 52−51.68 efficiently.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.
Steps: Start at 51.68 and count up 0.32 to 52.
Explain why counting up is shorter in this situation.

WorkedExamples.Title: Different decimal lengths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 102.5−8.06.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.
Steps: Subtract 8 whole units and six hundredths with necessary regrouping.

WorkedExamples.Title: Mix sum and difference
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 120+24.85 and 120−24.85.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.
Steps: For subtraction, use 120−25+0.15 or aligned columns.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use the same operation because adjacent exercises have the same decimal digits
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Addition and subtraction answer different quantity questions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Read each operator and estimate the expected magnitude before calculating.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use a long written algorithm even when a simpler justified method works
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The source is designed for strategy selection, not mandatory one-layout answers.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare a counting-up or compensation model and justify the method selected.

SummaryPoints: Exact decimal sums and differences can be checked using inverse operations.
Select and justify an efficient method based on number relationships.
Source discussion, optional challenges and method critique are teacher-reviewed.

Lessons.Title: Multiply Decimals and Whole Numbers
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: multiply a positive whole number by an amount of tenths or hundredths using repeated equal-sized parts, grids, whole-number products and place value. The source deliberately starts with easy grids before critiquing an imprecise student explanation that amounts to multiplying digits and assigning units.

Warm-up: describe two original full hundredths grids each with 40 hundredths selected; together they show 2×0.40=0.80 of one common unit. Explain why writing 80 hundredths equals eight tenths, not eighty entire wholes.

Activity 1 — gradually increase precision: calculate 3×0.6=1.8 as 18 tenths, 3×0.09=0.27 as 27 hundredths, and 3×0.69=2.07 as the sum 1.8+0.27. A learner may shade three diagrams of the same unit, use multiplication facts or present an accessible equal-parts description.

Activity 2 — critique incomplete reasoning: a classmate claims 'just multiply as if whole numbers and add a decimal' for 6×0.08. Ask the student to revise the explanation so it names 6 groups of 8 hundredths, hence 48 hundredths or 0.48. Contrast with 6×0.8=4.8 (48 tenths), and explain why the printed 8 occupies a different place in the two expressions.

Assessment: numeric products may be graded if the exact factors are supplied. Diagrams, the unit whole, the explanation of why the product has the right decimal place, and revisions of a peer's ambiguous method require teacher review.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole-number groups of tenths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply the count of equal groups by the tenths contained in each group.
KeyConcepts.Example: Eighteen tenths are one whole and eight tenths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Whole-number groups of hundredths
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply the number of groups by the hundredths contained in one group.
KeyConcepts.Example: Forty-eight hundredths are not forty-eight tenths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distribute mixed place values
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply tenths and hundredths separately, then add the two place-value contributions.

WorkedExamples.Title: Multiply tenths
WorkedExamples.Question: Three groups contain 0.6 each. Find the total.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.
Steps: Multiply three groups by six tenths to obtain eighteen tenths.
Compose ten tenths into one whole.

WorkedExamples.Title: Multiply hundredths
WorkedExamples.Question: Six groups contain 0.08 each. Find the total.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.
Steps: Calculate six times eight equals forty-eight hundredths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Use known products
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 3×0.69 by decomposing.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assign decimal places by a guess instead of naming place units
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: 'Multiply digits then put a decimal' does not explain whether the factor counts tenths or hundredths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the unit size of the repeated quantity and multiply number of units.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat three tenths as three whole units on the grid
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original whole contains ten tenths or one hundred hundredths.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Label both the fractional unit and the full unit square.

SummaryPoints: Each product can be interpreted as a whole-number count of tenths or hundredths.
Place-value language justifies a product's decimal size.
Teacher reviews diagrams and student method critique, beyond numeric products.

Lessons.Title: Use Whole Number Facts
ExplanationParagraphs: Learning goal: use the associative and distributive properties to rewrite a positive whole number times a decimal as exact whole-number products TIMES one tenth or one hundredth. The source first asks whether equations are true or false, and later asks for two different representations of the SAME source diagram.

Warm-up — truth and reasonableness: compare 5×0.6 with 30, and 4×0.08 with 32×0.01. The former is 3.0, not 30; the latter is 0.32 and correctly counts 32 hundredths. A whole number multiplied by a positive fraction less than one must yield a product less than that whole number.

Activity 1 — explain all place-value factors: calculate 7×0.04=(7×4)×0.01=0.28; contrast it with the incorrect 7×0.04=(7×4)×0.1=2.8. Complete an equation such as 8×0.7=(8×7)×___ with one tenth, and 8×0.07=(8×7)×___ with one hundredth. Explain why only the correct unit gives equivalent products.

Activity 2 — match two expressions to one model: an accessible hundredths diagram has four equal groups of 0.13, or a combined 52 hundredths. Interpret both 4×13×0.01=0.52 and 4×0.1+4×0.03=0.52, then critique the false shortcut 4×13×0.1=5.2. A student must describe the four grouped tenths-and-hundredths selections, not only calculate.

Assessment: false-equation critiques, blank-filling and diagram/expression matching can have numeric subchecks but the learner's justification and chosen interpretation are teacher-reviewed; original source visual and protected response not reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Associate whole facts with fractional units
KeyConcepts.Definition: Rewrite a decimal amount as an integer number of a named place-value fraction.
KeyConcepts.Example: The factor 0.01 is what makes 28 hundredths.

KeyConcepts.Title: Distribute across decimal places
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply tenths and hundredths contributions separately and add.

KeyConcepts.Title: Scale benchmark catches decimal errors
KeyConcepts.Example: The product must be less than seven.

WorkedExamples.Title: Whole-number fact with hundredths
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 7×0.04 and justify the decimal.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.

WorkedExamples.Title: Fill the unit blank
WorkedExamples.Question: What value completes 8×0.07=(8×7)×___?
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.
Steps: Write the unit one hundredth to make 56 hundredths.

WorkedExamples.Title: Match two expressions to one diagram
WorkedExamples.Question: A model shows four groups of 0.13. Find the sum using whole-number facts and distribution.
WorkedExamples.Method: First-party decimal model and independently checkable place-value computation, with teacher-reviewed justification.
Steps: Count 4×13=52 hundredths in the combined groups.
Or split each group into 0.1 and 0.03.

CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Seven tenths is 0.7, which is ten times as large.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Name the hundredth unit explicitly, not only the printed 7.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Accept a product larger than the positive whole factor without checking
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A positive multiplier below one produces a smaller positive product.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare to n×1 and verify the resulting magnitude.

SummaryPoints: Whole-number multiplication facts remain useful when the units are tenths or hundredths.
Associative and distributive properties provide two equivalent diagram interpretations.
Reasoned true/false statements and student diagrams remain teacher-reviewed.
